title: Quantum Federated Learning Based on Bures--Uhlmann Geometry for Heterogeneous Noisy Clients
authors: Haruki Emori, Masaki Uchihara, Yuuki Tokunaga
abstract: Quantum federated learning enables collaborative model training across quantum devices without sharing raw data, and it faces the data and hardware heterogeneity inherent to noisy quantum devices. Utilizing the quantum geometric tensor is a natural remedy, yet pure-state approaches and diagonal approximations discard the correlations that encode parameter incompatibility. To address this, we extend the parameter-space geometry to the mixed states that noisy clients actually prepare. The real part of the resulting mixed-state geometric tensor is the Bures metric, which measures how fast the physical state changes under parameter variation, and the imaginary part is the mean Uhlmann curvature, which quantifies the incompatibility of estimating multiple parameters simultaneously. Accordingly, we employ the Bures metric as a local preconditioner and use the mean Uhlmann curvature to develop an achievable-precision aggregation rule that dynamically down-weights unreliable clients. Furthermore, we establish theoretical guarantees by proving a convergence theorem and a variance-dominance proposition. Empirical evaluations on a trapped-ion quantum emulator demonstrate that the proposed method maintains high accuracy across diverse device-heterogeneity conditions and outperforms standard federated averaging, whose accuracy degrades under strong noise.
summary: This paper proposes an advanced framework for Quantum Federated Learning designed for noisy quantum hardware. It leverages the Bures metric and mean Uhlmann curvature—derived from analyzing mixed quantum states—to create a superior aggregation rule. This method dynamically weights clients based on their local noise and parameter incompatibility, leading to better model convergence than standard averaging techniques.
main_problem: Developing a robust aggregation rule for Quantum Federated Learning (QFL) that accurately accounts for data and hardware heterogeneity and noise in quantum devices.
main_result: The proposed method, utilizing the Bures metric and mean Uhlmann curvature, maintains high accuracy across diverse noise conditions and outperforms standard federated averaging, which degrades under strong noise.
method: The authors extend quantum geometry from pure states to mixed states, employing the Bures metric as a local preconditioner and using the mean Uhlmann curvature to develop a dynamic, precision-aware aggregation rule.
model_or_system: The model involves training variational quantum circuits (VQCs) on noisy quantum devices (NISQ era). Clients prepare mixed states $\rho_k(\theta)$ due to hardware noise, necessitating the use of mixed-state geometry.
key_observables: Bures metric (measures state change rate) and mean Uhlmann curvature (quantifies parameter estimation incompatibility).
important_parameters: Depolarizing rates (e.g., 0.4–0.6), data size ($p_k$), and local precision ($ho_k$).
main_assumptions: The core novelty is moving the geometric analysis from pure states to the mixed-state regime, which is necessary because pure-state approaches discard crucial correlation information.
figures_summary: The notes detail comparisons of aggregation weights (QFedQGT vs QFedFisher vs QFedAvg) and the final accuracy results on a trapped-ion quantum emulator.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, derives the mixed-state geometry (Bures-Uhlmann), proposes the local update (Bures metric) and aggregation rule (Uhlmann curvature), provides theoretical convergence guarantees, and validates the method via empirical simulation on a trapped-ion emulator.
why_interesting: It directly addresses the practical challenges of applying quantum machine learning algorithms to real, noisy hardware by incorporating advanced concepts from quantum information geometry into the optimization framework.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. One layer of the shared variational quantum classifier, drawn for three qubits, with the experiments using n = 6 and L = 3. Each layer re-uploads the data through Ry(xj) (green), applies a trainable single-qubit block RzRyRz (blue), and a linear CNOT entangler (pink). After L layers the Pauli observables (23) are measured in three settings (Z, X, Y ) and fed to the shared readout head (24). The three QFL methods use this same circuit and the same head, and differ only in the local update and the aggregation.

FIG. 2. Test accuracy against the communication round on MNIST-10 (n = 6 qubits, L = 3 layers, K = 9 clients), evaluated on the reimei-E trapped-ion emulator with 4000 shots per circuit and averaged over three seeds, with error bars the cross-seed standard error. Panels (a)–(d) are the four device-heterogeneity conditions of Table I, namely (a) few shots and strong noise, (b) more shots and strong noise, (c) few shots and weak noise, (d) more shots and weak noise. QFedQGT (solid, red) attains the highest round-averaged accuracy in every panel.
